Eager for revolution out of insolence, Lepidus was preparing to rescind the acts of so great a man; nor undeservedly, if only he could have done it without great calamity to the state.

For when Sulla the dictator had, by the right of war, proscribed his enemies, those who survived, when Lepidus recalled them, what else were they but summoned to war? And when the goods of the condemned citizens, by Sulla's assignment, though ill gotten, were yet held by right, the demand for them back beyond doubt was
shaking the settled condition of the state. It was expedient, then, for the sick and wounded state, as it were, to be quiet by any means, lest its wounds should be torn open by the very cure.
So, when by turbulent assemblies he had terrified the state as with a trumpet, having set out into Etruria, he was bringing arms thence and an army against the city.
But already Lutatius Catulus and Gnaeus Pompeius, the leaders and standard-bearers of the Sullan dominion, had occupied with another army the Mulvian bridge and the Janiculan hill.
Driven back by these at the very first onset, and judged an enemy by the senate, in a bloodless flight he withdrew into Etruria, thence into Sardinia, and there perished of disease and remorse.
The victors too, what was not lightly the case in civil wars, were content with peace.

The second discord, in the midst of the city, the lust of the decemvirate kindled. Ten leading men, chosen by the people's command, had drawn up laws brought from Greece, and all justice had been ordered in the Twelve Tables; yet they kept the rods of office handed to them with a kind of royal frenzy.

Above the rest Appius was carried away to such insolence that he marked out a freeborn maiden for outrage, forgetful both of Lucretia and of the kings and of the very law which he himself had composed.

And so, when Virginius the father saw his daughter, condemned by a sham judgement, being dragged into slavery, he hesitated not at all, but slew her with his own hand in the midst of the forum, and, bringing up the standards of his fellow soldiers, he dragged down that whole tyranny, beset by arms, from the Aventine hill into prison and chains.

The third sedition was stirred up by the dignity of marriage, that the plebeians might be joined with the patricians; which uprising blazed out on the Janiculan hill under the leadership of Canuleius, tribune of the commons. The fourth was the desire for office, that magistrates too might be created from the commons.
Fabius Ambustus, the father of two daughters, had given one to Sulpicius, a man of patrician blood,

and the plebeian Stolo had taken the other to himself. When she, on a certain occasion, was startled at the unfamiliar sound of the lictor's rods, unknown to her household gods, and was mocked somewhat too insolently by her sister, she could not bear the affront.
And so her husband, having obtained the tribunate, wrung from the senate, however unwilling, a share in the offices and magistracies.

But in these very seditions you would not undeservedly look up to the foremost of peoples. For it championed now liberty, now chastity, now the dignity of birth, now the honours and insignia of office, and amid all these it was the keener guardian of none than of liberty,
and could be corrupted by no bribe to surrender it, although, as in a great people and one daily growing greater, harmful citizens sometimes arose.

Spurius, suspected of bribery, and Cassius, suspected by his agrarian law of aiming at kingly power, it punished with instant death. And of Spurius indeed his own father exacted the penalty; the other, by the command of Quinctius the dictator, Servilius Ahala, master of the horse, stabbed in the midst of the forum.
Manlius, again, the saviour of the Capitol, because, having freed many of the debtors, he was lifting himself up too high and too lawlessly, it hurled from that very citadel which he had defended.

Such at home and abroad, such in peace and war, was the Roman people in that strait of its adolescence, that is, the second age of its empire, in which it subdued by arms the whole of Italy between the Alps and the strait.
